sugestoes.texto: WHAT: When a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot falls inside it, checkIfIsAvailable returns true right away and never runs the busy check. WHY: Existing bookings and calendar busy times are ignored on override days, so already-booked slots are offered and can be double-booked. HOW: Remove the early return so the busy.every check still runs; use dateOverrideExist only to skip the working-hours check.

WHAT: Two different Dayjs instances are compared with ===, which is reference equality and always false. WHY: A day-off override (start equals end) is never detected, so a slot starting exactly at the override time passes the later range checks and stays bookable. HOW: Use `.isSame()` to compare the two times.

WHAT: The end-bound check uses slotStartTime.isAfter(override end) instead of checking the slot's end time. WHY: A slot that starts inside the override but runs past its end (e.g. a 60-minute slot at 10:30 for a 10:00-11:00 override) is accepted, so a host can be booked outside their override hours. HOW: Reject the slot when slotEndTime is after the override end.

WHAT: The start-bound check only rejects slots that end at or before the override start; it never checks whether the slot starts before the override. WHY: A slot that begins before the override window and ends inside it is treated as available, so fixed hosts can be booked partly outside their override hours. HOW: Reject the slot when slotStartTime is before the override start.

WHAT: `end` is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, so it always equals `start`. WHY: Slots that start inside working hours but end after them (e.g. a 60-minute slot at 16:30 when work ends at 17:00) are not rejected. HOW: Compute `end` from slotEndTime.

WHAT: The working-hours check marks a slot unavailable if ANY working-hours range on that weekday does not contain it. WHY: Users with split availability (e.g. 9-12 and 13-17 on the same day) have every slot rejected, because each slot falls outside at least one range, so no slots are offered at all. HOW: Mark the slot unavailable only when no range for that day contains it (use some/every over the ranges for that day).

WHAT: The override date is formatted with `dayjs(...)`, which uses the server's local timezone, while the slot date is formatted in UTC. WHY: On a server not running in UTC, the day comparison is off for overrides near midnight, so overrides get applied to the wrong day or skipped. HOW: Use dayjs.utc(date.start) before adding the offset and formatting.

WHAT: After the timezone offset is added, startTime/endTime are computed as hour*60+minute, which wraps at midnight. WHY: For overrides that cross the invitee's midnight (e.g. 20:00-23:00 UTC shown to a +6:00 invitee), endTime ends up smaller than startTime, so buildSlots produces no slots or slots in the wrong part of the day. HOW: Compute minutes relative to the start of the invitee's day (e.g. diff in minutes from startOfInviteeDay) instead of taking hour/minute of the shifted time.

`end` is named for, and compared against, the end of working hours, but it is calculated from `slotStartTime`, which makes it identical to `start`. As a result, `end > workingHour.endTime` never catches a slot that starts inside working hours and runs past their end. Compute it from `slotEndTime` so the value matches its name.

`end` is calculated from `slotStartTime`, so it always equals `start`, and the `end > workingHour.endTime` check never catches a slot that runs past closing time. Example: with working hours 9:00-17:00 and a 60-minute event, a 16:30 slot is accepted even though it ends at 17:30. Calculate `end` from `slotEndTime`.

The end-side test only rejects slots whose start is strictly after the override end. A slot that starts exactly at the end, or that starts inside the override but runs past its end, is still treated as available. Example: with an override of 09:00-12:00 and a 60-minute event, slots at 11:30 and 12:00 are both accepted.

`end` is computed from slotStartTime, so it always equals `start`, and `end > workingHour.endTime` only fires when the slot starts after working hours end. Slots that start inside working hours but run past the end are wrongly treated as available. Compute `end` from slotEndTime.

`dayjs(...) === dayjs(...)` compares two different object references, so it is always false. A zero-length override (one that marks the day unavailable) is never caught by this branch. Use `.isSame()` to compare the instants.

The `find` returns true, which makes the slot unavailable, as soon as the slot falls outside any single override on that date. With several override ranges on one day (e.g. 9-11 and 14-16), a 14:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the 9-11 range. The slot should be rejected only when it fits in none of that day's override ranges.

This PR makes checkIfIsAvailable reject slots outside the user's date overrides and working hours. This call site looks up userSchedule but passes only its timeZone, so dateOverrides and workingHours fall back to []. Slots for this user are then checked only against busy times, unlike the other two call sites, which spread the user's schedule.

`dayjs(a) === dayjs(b)` compares two new object references, so it is always false. As a result, a date override that marks the day unavailable (start == end) is never rejected here. A slot starting exactly at the override's start passes both later checks and gets reported as available. Use `.isSame()` instead.

`end` is calculated from slotStartTime, the same value as `start`, so the `end > workingHour.endTime` check never looks at when the slot actually ends. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end is therefore accepted. Calculate `end` from slotEndTime.

`workingHours.find` returns a match as soon as the slot falls outside ANY working-hour entry for that weekday. With split ranges on one day (e.g. 9–12 and 13–17), a 14:00 slot is outside 9–12 and gets rejected, even though 13–17 contains it. The slot should be rejected only when no entry for that day contains it.

issues.descricao: The working-hours check computes end from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, so slots that start within working hours but end after them are accepted.
issues.textoGolden: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — an exact duplicate of `start` — instead of using `slotEndTime`. WHY: the working-hours upper-bound test `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore compares the slot START against the working-day end, so a slot whose start is inside working hours but whose end (start + eventLength) overruns `workingHour.endTime` is never filtered and is reported as available, allowing bookings outside the host's working hours. HOW: compute `const end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute();`.

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`, so it always equals `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` check is identical to the `start` check and never catches a slot that starts within working hours but ends past them. Use `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()` for `end`.

`end` is computed identically to `start` (both from slotStartTime), so the check `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` can never reject a slot on the upper bound. A slot starting inside working hours but ending after workingHour.endTime is wrongly considered available; derive `end` from slotEndTime instead.

issues.descricao: The date-override check compares two dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, so zero-length (day off) overrides are never detected.
issues.textoGolden: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

comentarios.texto: This compares two separately constructed dayjs objects with `===` (reference equality), which is always false, so a zero-length override (start equal to end, whole day blocked) never returns true here. Compare timestamps, e.g. `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))`.

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two separate dayjs object references, so `===` is always false. The zero-length date-override branch is dead code and such an override is never recognised as covering the day; compare values (e.g. .isSame() or .valueOf() === .valueOf()) instead.

The equality check compares two separately created Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, even when the override start and end represent the same instant. The intended zero-length/closed-day rejection is unreachable, and a slot beginning exactly at that instant can reach the dateOverrideExist success return. Compare timestamps or use isSame instead.

issues.descricao: When a date override exists for the day, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before checking busy times, so slots overlapping existing bookings are reported available.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: when `dateOverrideExist` is true the function returns `true` before running the `busy.every(...)` check at the end. WHY: on any day that has a matching date override, a slot inside the override is reported available without checking the host's existing bookings (`busy` is spread via `...schedule`/`...userSchedule`), so a fixed/loose host who already has a booking during the override window is still shown as free — enabling double-booking. HOW: do not return early here; fall through so the override branch only decides whether the slot is inside the override window, and let the existing `busy` evaluation decide availability (e.g. `if (dateOverrideExist) { /* within override, still check busy */ } else { /* fall through to busy */ }`).

The new `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` short-circuits the `busy` conflict check (and the workingHours check) for any slot that falls inside a date override window. Every caller of `checkIfIsAvailable` previously counted on it returning false for a slot that overlaps an existing booking; on days covered by a date override that guarantee is gone, so slots conflicting with the user's real bookings are now reported as available and can be double-booked. The override branch should let control fall through to the `busy.every(...)` check (returning true only for the availability-window part) instead of returning early.

A matching date override returns true before checking busy periods. Both fixed-host and loose-host callers pass calendar and booking conflicts in busy, so a host with an override is offered even when an existing booking overlaps the slot. Continue to the busy checks after validating the override instead of returning true.

issues.descricao: The working-hours check rejects a slot when any interval for the weekday excludes it, so split schedules (e.g. morning and afternoon) reject all slots.

comentarios.texto: The working-hours predicate rejects a slot if any interval on its weekday does not contain it. A split schedule of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 therefore loses every slot, since each valid slot lies outside the other interval. Require at least one matching interval to contain the full event instead of finding an interval that excludes it.

This search rejects a slot if it falls outside any working-hours window on that weekday. With split hours of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a valid 10:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the afternoon window. Check for containment in at least one applicable window rather than finding any window that excludes the slot.

WHAT: Outside-working-hours test uses workingHours.find() returning true if ANY entry rejects the slot. WHY: With split schedules (two entries same weekday, e.g. morning+afternoon) a valid morning slot is outside the afternoon entry, find() matches and the slot is wrongly rejected as outside hours. HOW: Invert logic to accept if ANY entry contains the slot (e.g. !workingHours.some(entry contains slot) => outside).

issues.descricao: The date-override bound compares the slot start, not the slot end, with the override end, so slots extending past the override are accepted.

comentarios.texto: The override bounds reject only non-overlapping slots rather than requiring the entire event to fit inside an override. A fixed host with a 10:00–11:00 override accepts a 10:30–11:30 event generated from another host's availability, despite being unavailable for its final half hour. Accept only when at least one override contains both slotStartTime and slotEndTime; this also avoids rejecting a slot merely because another interval on the same date does not overlap it.

The upper bound checks whether slotStartTime is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override end but finishes after it is treated as available. Compare slotEndTime with the override end using isAfter, so the slot must fit entirely inside the override.

issues.descricao: The override timezone conversion keeps only hour and minute, so overrides that cross midnight in the invitee timezone become inverted ranges or are applied to the wrong day.

comentarios.texto: Timezone conversion takes only hour and minute, discarding day rollover and turning intervals crossing attendee midnight into reversed ranges. A UTC organizer's 22:00–23:00 override viewed in UTC+01:30 becomes startTime 1410 and endTime 30, which buildSlots skips because start is greater than end, removing valid availability. Preserve the converted dates and split the interval across attendee-day boundaries before building slots.

WHAT: activeOverrides are filtered by UTC day (line 206-207) before the invitee/organizer offset is applied (lines 212-224), and shifted hours are not re-bucketed across midnight. WHY: An override that shifts to the previous/next calendar day in the invitee timezone is dropped from the wrong day or applied to the wrong day, so slots show open when the organizer is off (and vice versa). HOW: Filter/bucket overrides in the invitee-local date after applying the offset, or emit split entries spanning two invitee days.

issues.descricao: The new working-hours check does not reject slots on weekdays that have no working-hours entry, so those slots are treated as available.

comentarios.texto: A weekday with no matching working-hours entry falls through to the busy checks and is treated as available when there are no conflicts. In round-robin events, slots generated for a loose host can consequently include a fixed host whose schedule excludes that day. Reject slots unless a working-hours interval on the slot's weekday contains the event, when no date override applies.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: canManage() returns true when the caller has only the VIEW scope on all groups, because it passes AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW to hasPermission. WHY: GroupsResource (line 181) uses auth.groups().requireManage() to guard top-level group creation, so an admin granted only all-groups VIEW can create groups (privilege escalation). HOW: check only the MANAGE scope.

WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission looks up and returns groupResource.getId() (the internal resource id), but group resources are named by group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup) and hasPermission resolves them with findByName. WHY: the lookup always misses and falls back to the all-groups resource, and the returned set holds resource ids. JpaUserProvider then uses that set as a group-id filter, so user search and count return the wrong users, or none. HOW: pass and collect groupResource.getName(), as ClientPermissionsV2 does.

WHAT: canView(GroupModel) does not check canView() (the all-groups VIEW/MANAGE permission), and GroupsResource/GroupResource no longer short-circuit with canViewGlobal. When a group has its own resource, hasPermission evaluates only that resource. WHY: an admin with an all-groups VIEW permission is denied view (and the group is filtered out of listings) for any group that has a specific permission resource without the VIEW scope. HOW: return true early when canView() is true, as V1 does.

The new Javadoc for requireManageMembers was copied from requireManageMembership and still points to canManageMembership(GroupModel). The two checks grant access through different scopes (MANAGE_MEMBERS versus MANAGE/MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP), so the doc gives callers the wrong contract. Change the link to canManageMembers(GroupModel).
The @return tag says the method returns a "Stream of IDs", but the signature returns Set<String>. Change the text to say Set so the doc matches the return type.

V2 Groups resources are named after the group id, but this loop collects `groupResource.getId()` (the resource's internal UUID) and also passes that UUID to `hasPermission`. As a result, `findByName` finds nothing and the check falls back to the all-groups resource. The returned set (used as `UserModel.GROUPS` to filter users by group) also holds UUIDs that match no group. Use `groupResource.getName()` for both the permission check and the collected value, as ClientPermissionsV2 does.

AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource names each group resource after the group ID, and hasPermission looks it up with findByName. This loop instead passes groupResource.getId(), the authz resource's own UUID, both to hasPermission and into the set that UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource store as the UserModel.GROUPS filter. As a result, per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are not found and the user search is restricted to IDs that are not group IDs; use groupResource.getName(), which is the group ID, instead.

V2 group resources are named after the group ID (see resolveGroup), and hasPermission looks them up by name, but this loop uses groupResource.getId(), which is the authz resource UUID. The per-group lookup therefore fails and falls back to the all-groups resource, and the returned set holds resource UUIDs that callers put in UserModel.GROUPS to filter users by membership. Use groupResource.getName() so the lookup and the returned IDs are actual group IDs.

The global canManage() check passes when the caller has only the VIEW scope on all groups, so a view-only admin passes requireManage(), for example when creating top-level groups. canManage(GroupModel) accepts only MANAGE, so this global check should accept only MANAGE as well.

Group resources are created with the group ID as their name (`resolveGroup` returns `group.getId()`), but this loop uses the generated resource ID instead. That resource ID never matches the `findByName` lookup in `hasPermission`, which then falls back to the all-groups resource, and it is returned as a 'group ID' that the user search and count filters by (`UserModel.GROUPS`). As a result, VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions on a specific group are checked against, and filter users by, the wrong identifier; use `groupResource.getName()` instead (excluding the all-groups type resource).

Group resources are named after the group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup), but this loop returns groupResource.getId(), the resource's own UUID. It also passes that UUID to hasPermission, whose findByName lookup misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. Callers (UsersResource.searchForUser, getUsersCount, BruteForceUsersResource) use the result as UserModel.GROUPS group ids, so under V2 user searches and counts filter on the wrong ids and never match the intended groups. Use groupResource.getName() for both the permission check and the returned set.

Per-group resources are named by group ID, but this code passes `groupResource.getId()` (the resource UUID) to `hasPermission`, so `findByName` misses and the check falls back to the all-groups resource. The same resource UUIDs are added to `granted`, which ends up in the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute used to filter user searches, so that filter compares against IDs that are not group IDs. Use `groupResource.getName()` for both the permission check and the returned set.

`MgmtPermissionsV2.groups()` now returns `GroupPermissionsV2`, but `GroupResource` still calls `isPermissionsEnabled`, `resource`, `getPermissions` and `setPermissionsEnabled` (lines 326–359) from its management-permissions endpoints. Those methods now throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, so the endpoints fail with an unhandled exception, likely a 500, when V2 is active. Return a safe value (for example `false` from `isPermissionsEnabled`), or have the endpoints check for V2 and return a client error instead.

issues.descricao: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE, so an admin with only view permission on all groups passes manage checks such as group creation.
issues.textoGolden: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

comentarios.texto: The no-arg canManage() returns true when the caller holds only an all-groups VIEW permission (`hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`), whereas the per-group canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) requires MANAGE. WHAT: a caller with only the view scope on all groups is treated as having manage rights. WHY: canManage()/requireManage() gate group creation and other manage operations (e.g. GroupsResource.addGroup -> auth.groups().requireManage()), so a read-only viewer of all groups can create/manage groups — privilege escalation. HOW: drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() only returns true for MANAGE, aligning it with canManage(GroupModel): `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70) evaluates hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), identical to canView() at line 52, so a caller granted only the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is treated as a group manager. The per-group overload canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) correctly requires only MANAGE, and AdminPermissionsSchema defines MANAGE as the manage scope for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, so the two checks disagree. requireManage() therefore succeeds for read-only administrators, letting them create/update/delete groups, add subgroups and map group roles. Drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() checks MANAGE only.

WHAT: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() grants global manage on VIEW scope (hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)). WHY: A caller with only view-all-groups permission passes the manage check, allowing group creation/management reserved for manage. HOW: Check only MANAGE, e.g. hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE).

issues.descricao: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses the authorization resource id instead of the resource name (the group id) for both the permission check and the returned set, so per-group view-members grants are not resolved and user filtering gets wrong ids.
issues.textoGolden: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses authz resource IDs (groupResource.getId()) as group IDs and looks them up via findByName. WHY: Resource names equal group IDs (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId()), so findByName(resourceId) misses and the returned set contains unusable IDs, breaking user search/count filtering by group. HOW: Use groupResource.getName() like V1 does (resource.getName().substring prefix / name) for both the hasPermission lookup and the granted set.

findByType callback passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and granted set, but AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup defines resource name (not UUID) as groupId and hasPermission looks up via findByName(server, groupId). Use groupResource.getName() for both check and granted set, otherwise lookups miss to all-groups fallback and callers receive authz UUIDs instead of group IDs.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses groupResource.getId() for lookup and result collection, but V2 group resources are named with the group ID (resolveGroup returns group.getId()) and hasPermission does findByName. Use groupResource.getName() in both places to evaluate the correct per-group resource and to return actual group IDs.

issues.descricao: Per-group resources are created without the Groups type, so getGroupIdsWithViewPermission's findByType never sees specific group grants.

comentarios.texto: findByType(GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) does not enumerate the specific group resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource, because that method creates them without setting their type. Consequently, specific VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are omitted from the group IDs used for user counts and database filtering. Assign the Groups type to specific group resources and ensure the all-Groups resource is not treated as a model group.

issues.descricao: The user search filter still requires legacy 'group.resource.<id>' resources, so with V2 group permissions the members of authorized groups are excluded from user searches.

comentarios.texto: The new V2 group permission IDs are passed into a JPA filter that still requires a legacy group.resource.<groupId> authorization resource. JpaUserProvider.groupsWithPermissionsSubquery checks for that prefixed name, whereas AdminPermissionsSchema creates V2 group resources named only with the group ID, so authorized group members are excluded from user searches even with valid group IDs. Update the database filtering path to support V2 resource naming rather than requiring a legacy V1 resource.

issues.descricao: The new Javadoc for requireManageMembers points to canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers.

comentarios.texto: The javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false, but this method is the require-variant of canManageMembers, not canManageMembership. The text was copied from requireManageMembership above it. It should reference canManageMembers so the documented contract matches the method name and behavior.

The Javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. It should refer to canManageMembers(GroupModel), which is a different check, so the doc misdescribes the method.

Javadoc for requireManageMembers references canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers (copy-paste). Fix link to {@link #canManageMembers(GroupModel)} so the contract describes the method it guards.

issues.descricao: The Javadoc of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a Stream though the method returns a Set.

comentarios.texto: The Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a 'Stream of IDs', but the method returns Set<String>. Change the @return text to describe a Set of group IDs.
@return says 'Stream of IDs' but method returns Set<String> getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. Fix doc to 'Set of IDs' to match the signature.

The new @return documentation promises a Stream of IDs, but the method declares Set<String> and both implementations return sets. Describe a set of IDs instead, so the documented return contract matches what callers actually receive.

issues.descricao: GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission runs a full permission evaluation for every group resource on each user search and count, costing O(groups) policy evaluations per request.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The denial cache is checked before any permission source and is never invalidated when permissions change or a resource is created. WHY: If a Check on a UID runs before the dashboard/folder is created or before access is granted, the user keeps getting `Allowed:false` for the whole shortCacheTTL, even though the new permCache-miss database fallback would now allow it. That is the stale-deny behaviour this PR is meant to fix. HOW: Don't short-circuit on the denial entry when the database has never confirmed the resource exists. Or, simpler, drop the denial-cache short-circuit and rely on the refetch path, possibly with a much shorter TTL for denials.

WHAT: When the cached permission map exists but does not allow the resource, Check now ignores it and calls getIdentityPermissions, which always runs permissionStore.GetUserPermissions against the database. WHY: Each distinct denied resource (per user and action, per TTL window) now costs a full permission query, where before it cost none. Per-item checks over search/list results the user cannot access therefore cause O(N) database queries, and singleflight only merges concurrent calls with the same key. HOW: Refetch at most once per user+action within a short window, for example with a 'recently refreshed' marker on userPermCacheKey, instead of once per denied resource.

WHAT: userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_', and resource UIDs can contain '_', so different (name, parent) pairs produce the same key (e.g. name='a_b',parent='' and name='a',parent='b_'). WHY: A cached denial for one resource is returned for a different resource, wrongly denying access for the TTL. HOW: Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or length-prefix or encode each component.

WHAT: newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the remote authz client in a 30s authzlib LocalCache, while only the in-proc client was switched to NoopCache. WHY: In standalone/remote deployments, Check and List results are still served from the client cache. Newly created dashboards and folders and fresh grants stay invisible for up to 30s, so the server-side refetch logic never runs. HOW: Use NoopCache for the remote client too, or a cache that does not store denied results.

The comment says the permCache entry allows access to the dashboard to show that it is never checked, but the entry is set to `false`, which does not grant access. Because the comment disagrees with the code, the test does not show that the denial cache wins over a cached allow: it would pass even if the denial-cache lookup were removed. Set the value to `true` so the code does what the comment says.

The test is meant to show that the denial cache wins over a cached allow, but it seeds permCache with `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`, which denies access. With the permDenialCache lookup removed, Check would still return Allowed=false from the cached map or the store, so this test cannot catch a broken denial-cache path. Seed a real allow (`true`) so only the denial cache can make the result false.

userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_' and doesn't escape them, so (name="a_b", parent="") and (name="a", parent="b") produce the same key. A deny cached for one resource is then returned for a different resource the user may actually be allowed to access, until the TTL expires. Fix this by using a separator that can't appear in UIDs, or by escaping or length-prefixing each part.

The denial key joins name and parent with "_", but resource and folder UIDs can themselves contain "_", so different pairs map to the same key. For example, (name="a", parent="b_c") and (name="a_b", parent="c") both produce `..._a_b_c`, so a cached denial for one resource wrongly denies the other until the TTL expires. Use a separator that can't appear in UIDs, or a length-prefixed or escaped encoding of each field.

userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with "_", which UIDs may contain. For example, name="a_b"/parent="" and name="a"/parent="b" produce the same key, so a cached denial for one resource makes Check return Allowed:false for a different resource the user can access. Use a delimiter that UIDs can't contain, or a distinct, unambiguous prefix like ".perm_denial_", so the key identifies exactly one (name, parent) pair.

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins name and parent with "_", and Grafana UIDs may contain "_". Different resources can therefore share one key: (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") both become "..._a_b_c". A denial cached for one resource is then returned in Check for the other, so a user who has permission is denied until the TTL expires; the fix is to use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or to encode the fields.

issues.descricao: The denial cache key joins name and parent folder with underscores, so different name/parent pairs can collide and a cached denial for one resource denies another until TTL expiry.
issues.textoGolden: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

comentarios.texto: The denial cache key does not distinguish underscores inside resource and parent UIDs from its field separators. For the same namespace, user and action, (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") generate the same key, so denying the first request makes Check return false for the second even if its permissions explicitly allow it. Encode the components unambiguously, for example as a JSON tuple or length-prefixed fields.

The denial cache key is not injective: for the same namespace, user and action, `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same key. After the first request stores a denial, Check's new early cache return denies the second request without checking its permissions, even if it is allowed. Encode the components unambiguously (for example a JSON tuple or length-prefixed components) and add a test verifying that these two requests do not share a denial entry.

Make the denial-cache key encode component boundaries unambiguously (for example, length-prefix or serialize the components). For the same namespace, user and action, name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c` both produce the suffix `_a_b_c`. Underscores can occur in resource UIDs, so denying the first request caches a key that causes Check to immediately deny the second request without evaluating its permissions, even if that resource is allowed.

issues.descricao: The explicit denial-cache test seeds the cached permission as false instead of true, so it would pass without the denial-cache short-circuit and does not verify it.
issues.textoGolden: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

comentarios.texto: This test claims to prove the permDenialCache short-circuit (service.go:116-121) denies access, but it seeds the cached permission as map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} (a deny), contradicting its comment "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked". Because the cached set is already a deny, checkPermission returns allowed=false, the code falls through to the DB path, and the fake store also returns no permissions, so Allowed stays false. The assertion passes even if the entire permDenialCache early-return were deleted. Seed the cached permission as true (map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true}) so that only the denial-cache entry can force Allowed=false; otherwise the test does not verify the feature.

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the code sets the permCache entry to `false`, which is a deny. The test therefore does not show that the permission cache is skipped. Set the value to `true`, or change the comment to match.

The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test would still pass if the permDenialCache check were removed. permCache is seeded with dash1:false, not true as the comment claims, so the normal path also denies. Seed permCache with {"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} and a store that grants the permission, so Allowed=false can only come from the denial entry.

issues.descricao: A cached permission set that denies a resource always triggers a full DB permission reload, so checks over many inaccessible dashboards issue one query per resource instead of being served from cache.

comentarios.texto: Every distinct resource denied by the cached permission map triggers a reload of the entire user's action permission set, because the denial cache is resource-specific and a cached false result always falls through to getIdentityPermissions. Sequential checks of N inaccessible dashboards therefore execute N full permission queries and cache rewrites even with a current action-wide cache; getUserPermissions' singleflight only merges overlapping requests. Bound refreshes per user/action with a short refresh cooldown or generation marker so different resource misses can share a recent refresh.

issues.descricao: The Service struct comment listing its caches was not updated for the new permDenialCache field.

comentarios.texto: The struct doc comment still reads "// Cache for user permissions, user team memberships and user basic roles", but this PR added the new `permDenialCache` field (line 58). The comment no longer enumerates what the struct actually holds and misleads a reader about the new denial-cache field; update it to mention the permission-denial cache so the prose matches the fields.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: updateManyByCredentialId is called with an empty data object `{}`, and Prisma does not write @updatedAt when no field is being updated. WHY: SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is never bumped after the cache refresh, so the intended 'last refreshed' signal for this credential's calendars never changes. HOW: Pass an explicit timestamp, e.g. `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`.

WHAT: After a successful cache delete, the component does not invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. It only calls the optional `onSuccess` prop, which SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper forwards from an optional `props.onChanged`. WHY: When the parent does not pass onChanged, the dropdown keeps showing the old 'Last updated' timestamp and the delete option for cache that is already gone, until the page reloads. HOW: Add `onSettled` to invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, as the disconnect mutation already does.

WHAT: When the credential is missing or not owned, the handler throws a plain `Error` instead of a `TRPCError`. WHY: tRPC maps it to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500), so an expected authorization or not-found case shows up as a server failure and is logged as one. HOW: Throw `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: ... })`.

WHAT: `sed -i '' -E ...` uses BSD/macOS in-place syntax. WHY: On GNU sed (Linux), `''` is read as the sed script and the real expression as a filename, so the command fails and GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated when the key already exists. HOW: Use a portable form such as `sed -i.bak -E "..." "$ENV_FILE" && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"`.

The comment says this call refreshes `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, but it passes an empty `data` object. Prisma only applies `@updatedAt` when there are fields to update, so with `{}` the write is skipped and the timestamp stays the same. Set `updatedAt: new Date()` explicitly so the update actually runs.

`updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` passes empty `data` and relies on Prisma's `@updatedAt` to touch the rows. Prisma may skip the update or leave `updatedAt` unchanged when `data` is empty, so the timestamp would go stale after every cache refresh. Set the timestamp explicitly so the write always happens.

The cache_last_updated timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded "en-US" locale, so users of every other language see a US-style date (M/D/YY, 12h) inside their translated sentence. Use the user's locale from useLocale (i18n.language) instead.

The header warning says updatedAt is added without a default and that this fails on a non-empty table, but the statement below adds DEFAULT NOW(). The comment contradicts the migration and will mislead anyone reading it; remove the stale auto-generated warning.

This call relies on `updateManyByCredentialId(id, {})` refreshing `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, but the repository passes the empty `data` straight to `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany`. Prisma may not write `@updatedAt` when no fields change, so the timestamp may never update. Pass the timestamp explicitly so the update actually changes the row.

issues.descricao: fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId with an empty data object, so Prisma does not refresh the @updatedAt timestamp and SelectedCalendar.updatedAt never reflects the cache refresh.
issues.textoGolden: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data {} to bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. WHY: Prisma updateMany rejects empty data (validation error) or no-ops without touching @updatedAt, so the refresh path throws or silently leaves updatedAt stale. HOW: pass an explicit touch field e.g. { updatedAt: new Date() }.

Comment claims "Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt" but call passes empty object {} as data, so nothing is updated (Prisma updateMany with empty data is a no-op/error). Fix comment or pass { updatedAt: new Date() } to match the stated intent.

updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data {}. Prisma updateMany throws when data is empty, so this line throws on every resync after the cache write. Pass an explicit touch e.g. { updatedAt: new Date() } instead of {}.

issues.descricao: After deleting the calendar cache, CredentialActionsDropdown does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, so where no parent refetch callback is passed the stale cache status and delete action remain visible.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `deleteCacheMutation`'s `onSuccess` only calls `onSuccess?.()` and never invalidates the `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query, while the sibling `disconnectMutation` explicitly invalidates it in `onSettled`. WHY: the 'Cache Status' row in the dropdown is rendered from the cached `connectedCalendars` result; after deleting the cache the query is not refetched, so the deleted status/last-updated entry stays visible and stale in the UI. HOW: invalidate the query in the cache-deletion mutation as well, e.g. `const utils = trpc.useUtils(); onSuccess: async () => { ...; await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate(); }`.

WHAT: deleteCacheMutation onSuccess only calls onSuccess?.() and never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, unlike disconnectMutation onSettled. WHY: cacheUpdatedAt stays stale after deletion so UI keeps showing old Last updated and delete action until manual refetch. HOW: add onSettled invalidate of connectedCalendars like disconnect does.

Successful cache deletion does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query that supplies cacheUpdatedAt. The wrapper forwards only an optional parent onChanged callback and disables window-focus refetch, so the deleted cache continues to appear present with its old timestamp and delete action. Invalidate utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars on successful deletion.

issues.descricao: The cache 'last updated' timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded en-US locale instead of the user's locale, so non-US users see US-style dates in an otherwise translated label.
issues.textoGolden: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

comentarios.texto: The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded "en-US" locale (new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)), so every user — regardless of their locale — sees a US-style date/time while the surrounding label is translated. Use the app's locale-aware date formatting helper (the user's current locale) instead of pinning en-US.

Date format hard-coded to "en-US" via Intl.DateTimeFormat while surrounding strings use t()/useLocale. Users in other locales see US short date/time. Use the active locale from useLocale/i18n instead of hard-coding "en-US".

The cache timestamp is always formatted with "en-US", even though the surrounding label uses the user's selected translation locale. Users in other locales therefore see US month/day ordering and time conventions inside an otherwise localized message, potentially misreading the last-update date. Use the active application locale for Intl.DateTimeFormat instead of hard-coding en-US.

issues.descricao: The calendar cache migration keeps a generated warning saying updatedAt has no default and cannot be added to a non-empty table, although the SQL adds it with DEFAULT NOW().

comentarios.texto: This warning says updatedAt is added without a default and cannot be added to a nonempty table, but the migration actually supplies DEFAULT NOW(), explicitly handling existing rows. Remove or correct the warning so operators reviewing the migration are not incorrectly told that existing data makes it unsafe to run.

issues.descricao: The test-gcal-webhooks.sh cleanup function always exits 0, including when called from the failure paths, so the script reports success when the tunnel could not be set up.

comentarios.texto: `cleanup` always runs `exit 0`, and it is also called on the failure paths (rate limit hit, failed to extract the URL). The script therefore reports success even though the tunnel failed and GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL was never updated. Have `cleanup` take an exit code, and pass 1 from the failure paths.

cleanup() always ends in `exit 0`, and both failure paths (rate-limit at lines 46-50 and 'Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL' at lines 56-59) call cleanup. So a script named test-gcal-webhooks that did not actually obtain the tunnel URL / update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL still exits with status 0, letting any automation treat the run as successful even though the setup it verifies failed. On the failure branches the script should exit non-zero (e.g. `exit 1`) so failure is observable; only the SIGINT/SIGTERM interactive shutdown should exit 0.

issues.descricao: The webhook test script updates .env with the macOS-only `sed -i ''` syntax, which fails on Linux GNU sed and leaves GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL unchanged.
issues.textoGolden: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `sed -i '' -E 's|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|' "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD/macOS `sed -i ''` form. WHY: under GNU sed (typical Linux dev/CI environment) the empty `''` is consumed as the script operand and the command errors, so the existing `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` line is never replaced and the tunnel URL is not written to the env file. HOW: use a portable invocation, e.g. `sed -i.bak -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` (or branch on `uname`).

The environment update uses BSD sed's `-i ''` syntax, which fails with GNU sed on Linux. When GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL already exists, the script leaves the previous URL unchanged but still prints that it was updated, preventing webhooks from reaching the new tunnel. Use a portable replacement strategy or select the in-place syntax based on the available sed implementation and check its exit status.

When GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL already exists, `sed -i ''` uses BSD/macOS syntax and fails under GNU sed on Linux. The script nevertheless prints that the URL was updated and keeps the tunnel running, leaving webhooks configured with the old URL. Use a portable replacement approach (or select the appropriate sed syntax) and only announce success after the edit succeeds.

issues.descricao: deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error when the credential is missing or not owned by the user, so tRPC returns a 500 instead of a structured FORBIDDEN/NOT_FOUND error.
issues.textoGolden: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The reminder cancel/delete calls inside forEach are now fire-and-forget async calls. The old code awaited the prisma deletes through prismaPromises. WHY: The handler can respond before the reminder rows are flagged `cancelled` or deleted, and in a serverless runtime that work can be dropped, so the reminders of a cancelled booking still go out. HOW: Collect the promises returned by deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder and add them to the Promise.all that is already awaited.

WHAT: requestReschedule no longer awaits reminder cancellation (`await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)` was removed), and the async delete helpers are called without await inside forEach. WHY: The mutation can finish before the old booking's reminders are flagged `cancelled` or deleted, so reminders for the rescheduled booking can still be sent. HOW: Map the reminders to the returned promises and `await Promise.all(...)` them.

WHAT: All SendGrid cancel requests run inside one try, so the first failing `client.request` throws out of the loop and `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` never runs. WHY: No cancelled reminder is deleted in that run, and the same failing reminder comes back on every later run, so the reminders after it are never cancelled and those emails are sent. HOW: Put the try/catch around each reminder so one failure does not block the rest.

WHAT: The reschedule path calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true. That sends the SendGrid cancel right away and does not flag or delete the reminder row. WHY: The PR says immediate SendGrid cancels are what stopped working because cancelled batches accumulate. Rescheduling is a frequent path, so it keeps filling that list, while requestReschedule uses the deferred `cancelled` flag for the same case. HOW: Drop the `true` argument so the reminder is flagged `cancelled` and the cron cancels it.

The `immediateDelete` parameter suggests the reminder is deleted right away. When it is true, though, the function only cancels the SendGrid batch and returns, leaving the WorkflowReminder row in place. Callers like the reschedule path in handleNewBooking pass `true` and get orphaned rows, so either delete the row in this branch or rename the flag to something like `immediateCancel`.

The Prisma deletes are lazy and only run at the `Promise.all` after the loop, but the whole loop sits in one try. If any `client.request` throws, none of that run's deletes execute, including those for reminders SendGrid already cancelled, and every later run fails on the same reminder and leaves the cancelled rows in place. Put the try/catch around each reminder and await its delete right after its cancel succeeds.

When `immediateDelete` is true, the function cancels the SendGrid scheduled send and returns, so the WorkflowReminder row is never deleted. On reschedule (handleNewBooking.ts:968) no cascade removes these rows, so they stay as `scheduled: true` with no `cancelled` flag, even though the email will never be sent. Delete the row after the cancel request succeeds.

issues.descricao: Reminder cancel helpers are called without await inside forEach when bookings are cancelled/rescheduled or workflows edited, so the handler can return before reminders are cancelled or deleted and failures are unobserved.
issues.textoGolden: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: async deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder called inside forEach without collecting/awaiting promises. WHY: handler returns before cancels complete and rejections are unobserved, so cancellations are lost and reminder emails/SMS are still sent (same fire-and-forget pattern repeated in handleNewBooking:966, bookings.tsx:488, workflows.tsx:212/376/519/574).

Cancellation now delegates the database update/deletion to asynchronous reminder helpers without awaiting them, while removing reminder deletes from the awaited promise list. The handler can finish before cancelled flags or unscheduled-reminder deletions are persisted, allowing a subsequent scheduler run to schedule a cancelled booking's reminder and leaving cancellation work unfinished when a serverless invocation terminates. Collect and await the helper promises; apply the same correction to the modified rescheduling and workflow-update callers that discard these promises.

Await the reminder cancellation promises before completing the cancellation request. These helpers now own persistence of cancellation: email awaits a workflowReminder update and SMS awaits Twilio before deleting the row. The forEach discards their promises, and removing remindersToDelete from the awaited promise list removes the previous guarantee that reminder state is cleared before the handler returns. In a serverless request the outstanding operations can be interrupted after the response, leaving reminders active for a cancelled booking. Collect these helper promises and include them in the awaited Promise.all.

issues.descricao: The cron cancels SendGrid sends for cancelled reminders in one try around the whole loop, so one failing cancel aborts all remaining cancellations and the row deletions, and the failing row blocks later runs.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: remindersToCancel loop awaits SendGrid cancel per-reminder inside one try and only runs Prisma deletes after the loop, with no method filter. WHY: a single throw (e.g. null SMS referenceId sent as batch_id, or one SendGrid error) aborts the loop and skips Promise.all deletes, leaving all other cancelled emails still scheduled so they are still sent.

Successful cancellation records are only deleted after every SendGrid request in the loop succeeds. If a later request fails, the catch skips all queued Prisma deletions; the next run retries an already-cancelled batch, which SendGrid rejects with 400, and aborts before processing the remaining reminders. Await each reminder's database deletion immediately after its successful cancellation and isolate errors per reminder so one failed batch does not block the others.

Handle cancellation failures per reminder rather than around the entire batch. If one SendGrid request rejects (for example, for an expired or invalid batch ID), the loop exits before cancelling the remaining reminders, and Promise.all is never reached, so even earlier successfully cancelled reminders remain in the database. The failed record stays eligible for the next run and can repeatedly block other cancellations until their emails are sent. Execute each successful deletion and isolate failures so the worker continues processing the remaining reminders.

issues.descricao: Email reminders for cancelled bookings are only flagged cancelled and cancelled in SendGrid by the cron later, so reminders close to their send time can still be delivered.

comentarios.texto: Deferred cancellation includes reminders less than ten minutes from their scheduled send time, when SendGrid no longer permits cancellation. A booking cancelled in that interval is only marked cancelled locally by deleteScheduledEmailReminder, and the cron's POST is rejected, so its email is still delivered. Process cancellation before SendGrid's ten-minute cutoff and explicitly handle cancellations that arrive after that deadline rather than relying on this cron query to stop delivery.

issues.descricao: The cron cancels SendGrid scheduled sends one at a time with sequential awaits, which is slower than batching.

comentarios.texto: The new cancel loop performs a sequentially awaited SendGrid HTTP request (`await client.request(...)`) for each reminder returned by an unbounded `findMany` (no `take`), then deletes them. WHY: this is O(N) serial network round-trips per cron run; if many reminders are cancelled at once (e.g. a bulk event-type disable or booking cancellation wave) the cron handler can block for a long time on serial SendGrid latency. HOW: fan the independent SendGrid cancel requests out with `Promise.all`, and/or bound the query with `take` plus pagination, then batch the DB deletes.

WHAT: SendGrid cancel issued with sequential await inside for loop over remindersToCancel. WHY: cron blocks O(N) sequential network round-trips instead of parallel batch, materially slowing the hourly schedule job as cancelled backlog grows.

issues.descricao: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and its immediateDelete flag do not delete anything; the names no longer describe the behaviour.

comentarios.texto: `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and its `immediateDelete` flag no longer match what the code does. The default path only marks the reminder `cancelled: true`, and the `immediateDelete` path only sends a cancel request to the email provider. Neither path deletes the scheduled send or the row, unlike the SMS counterpart, which still deletes. Rename them (for example `cancelScheduledEmailReminder` and `immediateCancel`) or document the behaviour.

issues.descricao: deleteScheduledSMSReminder deletes the DB row only after a successful Twilio cancel, so a cancel failure leaves the reminder row behind now that callers no longer delete it.

comentarios.texto: twilio.cancelSMS and prisma.workflowReminder.delete share one try block. If the Twilio cancel throws, the DB row is never deleted. The reminder row then stays behind for a booking that was cancelled, rescheduled or deleted, because the callers no longer delete rows themselves. Delete the row in a finally block, or handle the cancel failure separately so the delete still runs.

issues.descricao: Prisma is imported in workflows.tsx but no longer used.

comentarios.texto: `Prisma` is imported as a value (line 9) but is no longer used anywhere in this file. This PR removed the only usages (`Prisma.BatchPayload` in the now-deleted `remindersToDelete` / `deleteReminderPromise` declarations), while the import was kept. WHY: the repo's ESLint `no-unused-vars` rule will fail CI/build for an unused import. HOW: remove `Prisma` from the import list (and keep `import type { PrismaPromise }` as a type-only import).

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Each `import()` in the appStore object literal runs as soon as the module loads, so all 28 app packages are fetched and evaluated immediately, and each one creates a promise with no rejection handler until some caller happens to await that key. WHY: Nothing is lazily loaded, so cold-start cost is unchanged. If any app module fails to load (missing env-dependent dependency, top-level throw), Node reports an unhandled rejection, which can crash the process even when that app is never used. HOW: Store loader functions (`applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and call them at lookup sites (`await appStore[key]?.()`).

WHAT: The forEach callback is now async and awaits getCalendar, so getCalendar errors and deleteEvent errors become rejected promises that forEach drops. WHY: Before, a synchronous getCalendar throw failed the requestReschedule mutation. Now it surfaces as an unhandled rejection after the response, and calendar deletions run detached and are never awaited. HOW: Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => {...}))`.

WHAT: Turning the forEach callback async moves the awaited getCalendar call out of the surrounding try/catch, because forEach discards the promise the callback returns. WHY: getCalendar failures that `logger.error` used to catch now become unhandled promise rejections, and the deletes are never awaited. The same change exists in wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts. HOW: Replace the forEach with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => {...}))` inside the try.

The callback is now `async` inside `forEach`, so the promises it returns are thrown away. Errors from `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` now surface as unhandled rejections instead of reaching the surrounding error handling, and the reschedule goes on before the old calendar events are deleted. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` so the code waits for the deletions and any failure is caught.

Now that getCalendar is async, the callback is an async function passed to forEach, so the returned promises are never awaited. Errors from loading or creating the calendar used to be caught by the enclosing try/catch; now they become unhandled rejections and the try/catch no longer catches them. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` so failures reach the existing catch.

The forEach callback is now async, so forEach drops the promise it returns. A rejection from `await getCalendar(...)` or from deleteEvent becomes an unhandled promise rejection instead of being caught by the surrounding error handling, and the mutation returns before the deletions finish. Map the refs to promises and await them with Promise.all (or loop with for...of and await), so failures are caught and run in order. vital/lib/reschedule.ts and wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts have the same pattern.

issues.descricao: Async callbacks passed to forEach after getCalendar became async are never awaited, so calendar and video cancellations run fire-and-forget, may not finish, and their errors escape the surrounding try/catch as unhandled rejections.
issues.textoGolden: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

comentarios.texto: The async forEach callback moves calendar factory exceptions outside the surrounding try/catch because forEach discards its returned promise. An invalid encrypted Exchange credential throws during CalendarService construction, now producing an unhandled rejection while Reschedule continues and returns success instead of logging the error; the identical regression occurs in wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts. Await Promise.all over bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...) inside the try block, or use an awaited for...of loop, so factory and deletion failures reach the catch.

The new async forEach callback is not awaited. If getCalendar rejects (for example, the dynamically imported calendar module fails to load or its service constructor throws), the callback produces a rejected promise that forEach discards; the surrounding try/catch cannot catch it. Previously a synchronous getCalendar failure reached that catch. Await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) or use an awaited for...of loop so these failures remain handled and calendar cleanup completes before rescheduling continues. Apply the same fix to the equivalent changed loop in wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts.

WHAT: credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { await getCalendar; apiDeletes.push(...) }) pushes to apiDeletes asynchronously after outer code consumes it. WHY: outer apiDeletes is awaited elsewhere while async callbacks have not yet pushed, so recurring-event deletions are lost/partial and errors are unobserved. HOW: replace with for...of with await or collect promises via map + await Promise.all.

issues.descricao: Each import(...) in the appStore object literal runs when app-store/index.ts is imported, so all integrations still load at startup instead of lazily, while every entry becomes a promise.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Targets are now run through applyTemplateVariables (with request.filters) before splitting, and they go through it again later. Each split sub-request (`{ ...request, targets }`) is sent through datasource.runQuery -> DataSourceWithBackend.query, which calls applyTemplateVariables again with the same scopedVars and filters (DataSourceWithBackend.ts:185). WHY: addFilterAsLabelFilter (modifyQuery.ts:511) does not check for duplicates, so ad hoc filters on parsed or structured-metadata labels are added twice (e.g. `{app="x"} | json | level=`info` | level=`info``), and variable values containing `$` are expanded a second time. The non-split path interpolates only once, so the two paths now send different queries. HOW: Clear the ad hoc filters on the sub-requests (e.g. build them with `filters: undefined`) or skip the second interpolation, so each query is interpolated exactly once.

WHAT: runShardSplitQuery now applies applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters) up front, but the sharded sub-requests keep request.filters/scopedVars. datasource.runQuery -> DataSourceWithBackend.query then calls applyTemplateVariables on them again. WHY: Ad hoc filters on non-indexed labels are appended twice by addFilterAsLabelFilter, which does not check for duplicates, and `$` sequences inside already-interpolated values are re-expanded, so sharded queries differ from what the user built. HOW: Remove `filters` from the sub-requests passed to runQuery, or make sure the backend-layer interpolation is not applied a second time.

The `.filter((query) => query.expr)` check now runs on the raw expr before `applyTemplateVariables`, whereas before this PR it ran after interpolation. A query like '$SELECTOR' whose variable resolves to an empty string now passes the filter and reaches shard splitting and runQuery with an empty expr. Move the expr filter after the map so the check applies to the interpolated value.

issues.descricao: Loki split/shard queries are now interpolated with applyTemplateVariables before splitting and again on execution, so ad hoc filters are applied twice and already-substituted values are re-interpolated.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (line 52), but it then delegates each sub-request to runSplitQuery (line 163), which this PR also changed to call datasource.applyTemplateVariables again (querySplitting.ts:299), so each target is interpolated (and ad hoc filters applied) twice. WHY: double interpolation re-runs addAdHocFilters on an already-filtered expression; the stream-selector path masks the duplicate via labelExists() dedup in addFilterToStreamSelector (modifyQuery.ts:494), but parsed/structured-metadata labels use addFilterAsLabelFilter which does not dedup, producing duplicated label filters, and any interpolated value containing '$' can be re-interpolated. This is confirmed by the updated test expecting applyTemplateVariables toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5) for a single target (1 call here + 4 sub-requests through runSplitQuery) instead of 1. HOW: interpolate only once — either remove the interpolation added to runShardSplitQuery and let runSplitQuery do it, or have splitQueriesByStreamShard pass the already-interpolated targets without re-interpolating in runSplitQuery.

The newly interpolated targets are interpolated again by DataSourceWithBackend.query when runQuery executes each split request. TemplateSrv.replace scans the resulting string again, so a variable whose literal value contains another defined variable token (for example, a log-search value containing `$other`) is expanded a second time and produces a different query from the non-splitting path; shard splitting also passes through this additional interpolation. Preserve the early interpolation needed for partitioning while ensuring already-interpolated targets are not interpolated again on execution, and test through the real backend query preparation rather than mocking runQuery.

Targets are interpolated here with `applyTemplateVariables`, including ad hoc filters, and then sent to `datasource.runQuery`, which interpolates them again through the backend path (datasource.ts:324/377). The ad hoc filters may be injected twice, and already-substituted values are re-interpolated, which can produce wrong or invalid LogQL. Interpolate only once. Either clear `scopedVars` and `filters` on the sub-requests after the first pass, or skip interpolation in `runQuery` for already-interpolated requests. The same issue applies to shardQuerySplitting.ts:52.

issues.descricao: runShardSplitQuery now filters empty/hidden targets before interpolation, so an expr that interpolates to an empty string is no longer dropped.

comentarios.texto: The order of operations was inverted relative to the previous contract: interpolation used to run before the `expr`/`hide` filters (interpolateVariablesInQueries(targets).filter(...)), and now the filters run on the *raw* targets before `applyTemplateVariables` is applied. Filtering on the un-interpolated `query.expr` means the previous fallback that dropped a target once variable substitution had emptied its expression no longer exists: a target like `{ expr: '$myVar' }` whose variable resolves to '' is truthy at filter time, survives, is then interpolated to `''`, and is passed into the shard splitting/execution loop as a blank query. To preserve the old contract the filters should run on the interpolated result (or the interpolated expr should be re-checked for emptiness).
